names.value: Baijie 白姐 means roughly 'White Sister'; as a Buddhist goddess she is Shengfei 圣妃, 'Holy Consort', while her mortal-mother form is Baijie Amei 白姐阿妹, 'Little White Sister', and her widow-martyr form bears the personal name Cishan 慈善, 'Kindness'.

sources.claim: Baijie Shengfei is a multiform Bai goddess of the Dali region, attested successively as the Buddhist consort of Mahakala, as Baijie Amei the mother of the kingdom's founder Duan Siping, as the widow-martyr Cishan, and as a contemporary village benzhu.

claims.notes: Baijie is the most studied goddess of the Bai, worshipped only in the Dali region. Megan Bryson traces four historical guises: a Buddhist goddess and consort of Mahakala in the Dali-kingdom ritual text Dahei tianshen daochang yi; Baijie Amei, a plum-born maiden who conceived the dynasty's founder Duan Siping after touching a dragon, a legend that crystallised in the fifteenth century under the Ming; the chaste widow-martyr Cishan (Baijie Furen), who identified her burned husband by an iron bracelet after the Nanzhao king's massacre at the Pine-Torch Tower and then took her own life; and a tutelary village benzhu venerated chiefly by older women today. The widow-martyr account is preserved in the Bai song of the Burning of the Pine-Torch Tower, the legend that the Bai attach to the Torch Festival.

claims.notes: Duan Siping (893-944) founded the Dali Kingdom in 937 and ruled as its first king. In Benzhuism, the indigenous patron-god religion of the Bai people of the Dali region, he is enshrined as the benzhu of the Duan family's home village at Qingdong near Xizhou, one of the deified rulers and ancestors whose worship knits each village to its history. A Ming-era legend made him the son of Baijie Amei, a maiden born from a plum who conceived him after touching a dragon, a motif that lent the founder of Dali divine paternity while giving his mother her own miraculous origin.

claims.notes: Duan Zongbang was a leading member of the Duan clan during the Nanzhao Kingdom, serving as chief minister and general; tradition credits him with campaigns in upper Burma and with bringing a Buddha-tooth relic to Dali. Posthumously he became the most exalted of the Bai patron gods, the Central Benzhu, said to rule the Five Hundred Divine Kings of the region, and was honoured as a remote ancestor of the royal Duan house that later founded the Dali Kingdom.

claims.notes: Mahakala, the 'Great Black Heaven-God' or Black Sky God, is a wrathful Buddhist guardian who became the focus of a flourishing cult in the Nanzhao and Dali kingdoms of Yunnan from the ninth century onward, appearing many-armed in the Jianchuan grottoes and as the chief deity of the Dali ritual manual Dahei tianshen daochang yi, in which his consort is the goddess Baijie Shengfei. In later Bai village religion the Black Sky God was absorbed into Benzhuism and is among the most widely enshrined of the protector benzhu of northwestern Yunnan.

linguistic.etymology: ᬪᬝᬵᬭ​ᬕᬸᬭᬸ Bhaṭāra Guru, the high-god (Śiva as supreme teacher). Both elements are Sanskrit loans. Bhaṭāra (भट्टार / भट्टारक bhaṭṭāraka) 'venerable lord, his worship, noble one' — an Indic honorific that in Old Javanese/Balinese became the standard title 'divine lord, deity' (batara/betara). Guru (गुरु) 'teacher, spiritual preceptor; heavy, weighty, venerable.' Together 'the Divine Lord (who is) Teacher / Lord Preceptor,' i.e. Śiva as cosmic guru. His Balinese name Sang Hyang Manikmaya likewise uses Sanskrit-derived maṇi 'jewel' + māyā. The loan path is Sanskrit → Old Javanese → Balinese.

linguistic.etymology: ᬤᬾᬯᬶ​ᬲ᭄ᬭᬷ Dewi Śrī, the rice-goddess. Both words are Sanskrit loans. Dewi < devī (देवी) 'goddess.' Śrī (श्री) is the Sanskrit name of the goddess of prosperity, fortune and abundance (consort of Viṣṇu, = Lakṣmī), the word also meaning 'splendour, radiance, auspiciousness, wealth.' In Indonesia Śrī was identified with the indigenous rice/fertility deity, so Dewi Sri is 'the Goddess Śrī,' the divine personification of rice and household abundance. Her Balinese epithet Nini Pantun 'Grandmother Rice-plant' (pantun 'rice-plant') is native. The core name derives from Sanskrit Śrī.

sources.reference: Gonda, Sanskrit in Indonesia, 2nd ed. (1973), s.v. śrī

linguistic.etymology: ᬭᬂᬤ Rangda, the demon-queen (a Durgā-aspect). The name is the Old Javanese word raṇḍā / rangda 'widow' — itself a loan into Old Javanese from Sanskrit raṇḍā (रण्डा) 'widow, a barren or wanton woman.' Applied to the witch-queen (historically associated with the 11th-c. widow-sorceress Calon Arang of the Calon Arang tale), the name literally means 'the Widow,' the dangerous unattached woman wielding black magic. The Sanskrit source raṇḍā 'widow' is securely the etymon of Old Javanese/Balinese rangda.

Among the Toba Batak the title is reassigned to one of the three primal gods (the Debata na Tolu); the Sanskritic name reflects the Indianised stratum of Batak religion rather than a native Batak coinage.

linguistic.etymology: Bathou Bwrai is the Bodo (Boro) supreme creator: Bathou is analysed as Bodo ba 'five' + thou 'deep/profound (principle)', i.e. 'the five profound principles' (the five elements dwi water, ha earth, bar air, okhrang sky, or fire), while Bwrai means 'elder, old man' (the eldest in power/knowledge). claims.notes: PROBABLY THE MOST WIDELY VENERATED FIGURE IN BUDDHISM AND THE BUDDHIST KEY HELD NOTHING OF HIM — while the corpus DOES hold chinese_guanyin, under the Chinese key. That is not a duplicate of this record and this batch does not make one: the East Asian Guanyin is a distinct cultic development with her own iconography and her own tradition, filed where she is practised, and the Indian Avalokitesvara of the eight great bodhisattvas is filed here. NO EDGE IS DRAWN between them, on the rule this programme has applied since lane 13, and the Chinese record is a census row. The other language-forms - Chenrezig, Kannon - are carried as aliases because the corpus holds no record under those keys; if a Tibetan or Japanese pass ever creates one, the alias is what will surface the overlap, which is exactly how lane 25's Umbu duplicate was caught. TYPE deity IS THE NEAREST CATEGORY THIS SCHEMA HAS AND THE TRADITION DOES NOT USE IT. Buddhism does not regard a Buddha or a bodhisattva as a god; the devas this corpus already holds under the Buddhist key are, in this tradition's own view, unenlightened beings inside samsara, and the figures in this block stand above them precisely by NOT being gods. The record says so rather than letting the type field make the claim.

claims.notes: Batara Guru, whose Bugis name is La Togeq Langiq, is the eldest son of the supreme god Patotoqe and his consort Datu Palingeq. He is the first of the manurung, the sky-descended beings: dispatched from the Upperworld Boting Langiq to the empty land of Luwuq, he becomes the first human and the first ruler of the Middleworld (Ale Lino), and in popular tradition he descends through a hollow stalk of golden bamboo, whence the epithet Manurungnge ri Lappa Tellang Pulawengnge. The title Batara Guru itself is a Bugis adaptation of the Sanskrit Bhaṭāra Guru, an epithet of Śiva, reflecting older Indic influence on the region. He takes as his bride We Nyiliq Timoq, who rises from the Underworld; their union joins the upper and lower worlds, and the dynasty descending from them — through their son Batara Lattuq to the hero Sawerigading — drives the action of the entire epic.

claims.notes: I La Galigo is the son of the hero Sawerigading and the princess I We Cudai of Cina, and grandson of Batara Lattuq of Luwuq. Though the sprawling epic cycle bears his name, he is in fact a comparatively late figure within it, a seafaring prince famed for gambling, cockfighting and roving adventures across the archipelago. His birth was marked by his mother's initial rejection of him. In Bugis reckoning he belongs to the last of the wholly divine-descended generations before the gods withdrew and the manurung ancestors of the historical dynasties appeared. The written cycle, Sureq Galigo, is among the longest literary works known.

claims.notes: Patotoqe, also called Datu Patoto and by the epithet To Palanroe ('the Creator'), is the highest deity of the pre-Islamic Bugis pantheon as preserved in the Sureq I La Galigo of South Sulawesi. Enthroned in the Upperworld Boting Langiq, he is the apportioner of fate (toto) for gods and mortals alike. When his counsellors report that the Middleworld lies empty between sky and sea, Patotoqe summons the rulers of the realms and resolves that it must be inhabited by beings of divine descent; he sends his eldest son Batara Guru down to the land of Luwuq to become the first human ruler, and arranges a bride for him from the Underworld. He stands at the head of the genealogy from which the entire human world of the epic descends.

claims.notes: Sawerigading is the great hero of the Bugis La Galigo cycle and its central human figure, a prince of Luwuq descended in the third generation from the sky: he is the grandson of Batara Guru and We Nyiliq Timoq (through their son Batara Lattuq) and thus the great-grandson of the supreme god Patotoqe. Coming of age, he falls in love with his twin sister We Tenriabeng, but their union is forbidden as an incest that would destroy the realm; the twins are parted, and Sawerigading vows to seek a bride who resembles her. To this end the colossal tree Welenrengnge is felled — the episode Ritumpanna Welenrengnge — and from its timber his great ship is built, in which he voyages as far as China to win the princess We Cudai, who is said to resemble We Tenriabeng. Their son is I La Galigo, after whom the whole epic is named. As a seafaring, restless, formidable captain who crosses the upper, middle and lower worlds, Sawerigading became the archetypal Bugis culture-hero, and is associated in tradition with the founding line of the kings of Luwuq.

Together they rule the depths of the waters and mirror below the world the sovereign couple Patotoqe and Datu Palingeq who rule above it. It is these two underworld deities who, jointly with the Upperworld gods, resolve to fill the empty Middleworld, and Sinaung Toja is accordingly counted mother of We Nyiliq Timoq, whose ascent and marriage to Batara Guru inaugurates human kingship in Luwuq.

claims.notes: We Nyiliq Timoq is the divine princess of the Underworld in the Bugis La Galigo cycle, the eldest daughter of the rulers of Pérétiwi — the undersea lower world also called Boriq Liu. When Patotoqe sends his son Batara Guru down from the sky to the empty land of Luwuq, a consort is sought for him in the depths, and We Nyiliq Timoq rises from beneath the sea to become his bride; she is also reckoned his cross-cousin within the divine kindred. Her ascent from below mirrors Batara Guru's descent from above, so that their marriage unites the Upperworld and the Underworld in the Middleworld of humankind. From this union descends Batara Lattuq, and in turn the hero Sawerigading and his twin We Tenriabeng, making her one of the apical ancestresses of the epic's human world.

claims.notes: We Tenriabeng is the twin sister of the hero Sawerigading, born to Batara Lattuq of Luwuq. Because a prophecy foretold that the twins would fall fatally in love, the bissu priests ordered them parted at birth, and We Tenriabeng was raised apart from her brother. When Sawerigading, returning home, does indeed conceive a forbidden passion for her, she wisely redirects him by describing her mirror-image, the princess I We Cudai of Cina, whom he departs to woo. We Tenriabeng herself renounces earthly marriage and ascends to the Upperworld (Boting Langiq), where she weds her celestial betrothed Remmang ri Langi. She is closely tied in the tradition to the bissu, the androgynous priesthood that mediates between the human world and the gods.

linguistic.etymology: သိကြားမင်း Thagya Min, 'King of the Nats,' the heaven-king who heads the nat pantheon. Min (မင်း) is native Burmese 'king, lord.' Thagya (သိကြား) is the Burmese form of Pali Sakka / Sanskrit Śakra (शक्र) — i.e. Indra, lord of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven — the Buddhist heaven-king; the Burmese pronunciation Thagya reflects Pali Sakka. So Thagyamin = 'King Sakka/Śakra,' the Indianized celestial sovereign equated with Indra, naturalized as the indigenous nat-king. The loan path is Sanskrit Śakra / Pali Sakka → Burmese Thagya.

linguistic.etymology: Buryat Esege Malaan (Tengri), literally 'Father Bald (Sky)'. Esege means 'father'; malaan means 'bald, bare', here understood of the open, cloudless sky, so the epithet is read both literally 'Bald-Headed Father' and figuratively 'Father of the Clear/Cloudless Sky'. In Buryat the related expression malaan tolgoiton 'bald-headed' was popularly extended to mean 'wise-headed', which colours the figure as a venerable patriarch.

After Khormusta vanquishes and dismembers the eastern khan Atai Ulan, whose scattered body engenders the demons and monsters of the middle world, the western tengri send Geser down to be born among humans and rid the earth of those evils. linguistic.etymology: Mongolic Qormusta / Khormusta (Tengri) is a naturalized loan from the Iranian theonym Ahura Mazdā. claims.notes: Strict ½ demigod — the cleanest East Asian match for the registry's strict criterion (deity mother Sanshengmu + mortal father Liu Yanchang, divine status of the mother holding under both traditions of her parentage). Canonical filial-piety hero of late-imperial Chinese popular culture; the Bao Lian Deng cycle is the most reproduced mother-rescue narrative in the corpus. Mountain-cleaving rescue inherits the narrative template directly from Erlang Shen — both demigods use the same Heaven-Splitting Axe to free an imprisoned divine mother, marking Chen Xiang's cycle as Erlang's structural sequel. In the Erlang's-sister tradition stratum the inversion is sharper: Erlang freed his mother from celestial imprisonment, Chen Xiang frees his mother from imprisonment imposed by Erlang himself, making nephew and uncle structural mirrors. Per Bao Lian Deng (Tang folk-cycle, Yuan-Ming drama); 1999 Shanghai Animation Film Studio adaptation.

'sinking fragrance,' the Chinese name for aloeswood/agarwood (Aquilaria resin, so dense it sinks in water): 沉 chén 'to sink, submerge' (Middle Chinese *drim) + 香 xiāng 'fragrance, incense, aromatic' (MC *xjang). The compound 沉香 is the ordinary lexical word for aloeswood, transparent in both elements.

variants.description: Alternate origin tradition identifies Erlang as Li Erlang (李二郎), second son of the Qin-dynasty hydraulic engineer Li Bing (李冰), governor of Shu (蜀, Sichuan) c. 256 BCE who built the Dujiangyan irrigation works. Under this variant Erlang's parentage is two mortals (Li Bing + unnamed wife) rather than deity + mortal — failing the strict demigod criterion. The Li Erlang tradition reflects historical-engineer apotheosis (the deification of Li Bing's work in Sichuan local cult) and was later conflated with the Yáng Jiǎn tradition at Guankou.

claims.notes: Strict ½ demigod under the dominant literary tradition (Yáojī + Yáng Tiānyòu); the Li Erlang variant (Li Bing's son, mortal-mortal) is recorded as secondary. Canonical narratives: cleaves Mount Tao with the Heaven-Splitting Axe to free his imprisoned mother (the foundational mountain-cleaving template that the Chen Xiang cycle later reproduces); subdues Sun Wukong during the Havoc in Heaven (Xiyou Ji 6-7); assists King Wu of Zhou in the Investiture of the Gods Shang-Zhou transition campaign. Distinctive iconography: vertical third eye in forehead, three-pointed double-edged blade, the Howling Celestial Dog, the Heaven-Splitting Axe. Post-deeds canonization as Qingyuan Miaodao Zhenjun installs him in the Daoist celestial bureaucracy under his uncle the Jade Emperor — the demigod-to-deity transition is recorded in the lifecycle array. Per Investiture of the Gods (c. 1605); Journey to the West (1592); Erlang Baojuan; Bao Lian Deng.

claims.notes: Supreme deity of the folk-Daoist pantheon; Lord of Heaven in the institutionalized Tang-Song imperial-state religious framework. The Jade Emperor presides over the celestial bureaucracy that mirrors the imperial-state administration — Heaven's Court is structured as the Chinese imperial bureaucracy with celestial officials, regional administrators, and ranked deities reporting to the Jade Emperor. Tang-period institutionalization by Emperor Xuanzong (713-756 CE) elevated the figure from local-folk-religion to imperial-state pantheon supremacy; the Song-period elaborated the celestial-bureaucracy framework. The Jade Emperor's birthday on the 9th day of the 1st lunar month (Tian Gong Sheng) is one of the major festivals of the Chinese folk-Daoist calendar, widely observed in Taiwan, Singapore, Malaysia, and other diaspora communities. The figure exists in productive tension with the older Heaven (Tian) abstraction of the Zhou-Confucian frame and with the Three-Pure-Ones (San Qing) Daoist-cosmological-supreme triad — the Jade Emperor is supreme in folk-Daoist pantheonic-administrative practice while the Three-Pure-Ones are theologically-cosmologically prior in formal Daoist theology.

sources.reference: Reference treatment of Zhinü, Niulang and Yue Lao: Niulang the Cowherd and Zhinü the Weaver Girl are the central figures of the Qixi story; Zhinü is a goddess skilled at weaving colourful clouds, the daughter of the Jade Emperor and the goddess of weaving, whose star is Vega, while Niulang is the star Altair in Aquila. Zhinü came down to Earth and, while bathing in a river, met Niulang; he stole her clothes, and unable to return to heaven without them she decided to marry him. When the heavenly queen found out about their union she tore them apart, condemning them to live on opposite sides of the Milky Way. Qixi is celebrated on the seventh night of the seventh lunar month, when a bridge of magpies forms across the sky for the lovers to cross. Yue Xia Laoren, the old lunar matchmaker god, is the Taoist deity in charge of the red thread and of marriages, typically represented with a staff in his right hand, a marital register in his left, and red thread draped over his arms.

relations.subject: chinese_sanshengmu

sources.reference: Bao Lian Deng; Erlang Baojuan stratum

relations.notes: In the Erlang's-sister tradition stratum (later than the independent Mount Hua goddess tradition), she is full sister of Erlang Shen — both children of Yáojī and Yáng Tiānyòu. Erlang himself imprisons her beneath Mount Hua to enforce the celestial prohibition on her mortal union, making the Chen Xiang cycle a mirror-inversion of Erlang's own freeing of Yáojī. The conflation is structurally significant — see variants for the tier-question.

variants.description: In the Bao Lian Deng tradition Sanshengmu is identified as Erlang Shen's full sister, daughter of Yáojī and Yáng Tiānyòu — under which reading she would be a strict ½ demigod (same parentage as Erlang) rather than an independent deity. Registry treats this as a secondary stratum because the older Bao Lian Deng cycle treats her as the established Mount Hua goddess descending to a mortal — same descent pattern Yáojī enacts when she takes Yáng Tiānyòu, with her divine status pre-existing the union. The Erlang's-sister identification appears to come from later attempts to unify the Erlang and Sanshengmu cycles into a single family tree. Adopting it as primary would privilege late euhemerizing accretion over earlier independent-goddess attestation.

sources.reference: Bao Lian Deng; Erlang Baojuan stratum identifying Sanshengmu as Erlang's sister

claims.notes: Chinese goddess of Mount Hua; mother of Chen Xiang by the mortal scholar Liu Yanchang. Registry treats her as deity (consistent with the older Bao Lian Deng stratum where she is the established Mount Hua goddess descending to a mortal — the same descent-to-mortal pattern Yáojī enacts in the Erlang cycle). The later Erlang's-sister identification (which would make her a ½ demigod with same parentage as Erlang Shen) is recorded in variants as secondary — adopting it as primary would privilege late conflation over earlier independent-goddess attestation. Imprisoned beneath Mount Hua by her brother Erlang (in the conflated tradition) or by celestial decree (in the older tradition); freed when Chen Xiang cleaves the mountain with the Heaven-Splitting Axe — the narrative template inherited from the Erlang precedent within Chinese popular religion.

claims.notes: Goddess of Mount Kunlun in the western mythological geography; goddess of immortality, fertility, and longevity; controller of the peaches of immortality (pantao) that grow on the cosmic Mount Kunlun and ripen every 3,000 years. The figure exhibits one of the most-distinctive iconographic transformations in Chinese mythology: in the earliest strata (Shanhaijing, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE), Xiwangmu is depicted in semi-bestial form (tiger-teeth, leopard-tail, jade-piped voice, dishevelled hair); in the later Han-Tang strata, she is rationalized into the imperial-court-style Queen Mother figure presiding over the peach-of-immortality banquets. The transformation reflects the broader Han-period rationalization of pre-Han mythological material into the imperial-bureaucratic-cosmological framework. The Tang-Song-period peach-of-immortality banquet narrative — at which Xiwangmu hosts the celestial gods at her Mount Kunlun palace and serves the peaches that ripen every 3,000 years — became a foundational topos of Chinese literature, painting, and theater (notably the Sun Wukong / Journey to the West episode in which Sun Wukong steals the peaches). Some scholars (Cahill 1993) connect the figure to broader Inner Asian-Eurasian goddess complexes (Saka/Scythian goddess parallels), reflecting potential Bronze-Age cultural-contact substrate.

domains.notes: Dwells on Kunlun; her archaic form had a leopard’s tail and tiger’s teeth.

linguistic.etymology: Chinese 西 Xi ("west"; the western direction in Chinese cosmological cardinal-direction system) + 王母 Wang Mu ("Queen Mother"; wang "king/queen" + mu "mother"). Literally "Queen Mother of the West." The west-direction encodes both geographical (Mount Kunlun is in western China) and cosmological (the west is the direction of yin, autumn, metal, white tiger, and the descending-Sun) dimensions. Some scholars (Cahill 1993) connect the Xiwangmu figure to broader Inner Asian-Eurasian goddess complexes (Saka/Scythian goddess parallels).

linguistic.etymology: 瑤姬 Yáojī, the celestial 'Jade Lady' of Mount Wu (Wushan). The name is descriptive: 瑤 yáo 'fine jade, precious jade-like stone, lustrous' (Middle Chinese *yew) + 姬 jī 'lady, beautiful woman, princess; an old surname-element and honorific for noblewomen' (MC *kjɨ) — 'Jade Lady / Lustrous-Jade Maiden.' Her alternate name 雲華 Yúnhuá means 'Cloud Splendor / Cloud-Blossom' (雲 yún 'cloud' + 華 huá 'flower, splendor, efflorescence'), evoking the clouds and rain of the Wushan goddess of the famous Gaotang rhapsody. Both names are transparent literary epithets.

relations.subject: chinese_zhinu

sources.reference: Reference treatment of Zhinü, Niulang and Yue Lao: Niulang the Cowherd and Zhinü the Weaver Girl are the central figures of the Qixi story; Zhinü is a goddess skilled at weaving colourful clouds, the daughter of the Jade Emperor and the goddess of weaving, whose star is Vega, while Niulang is the star Altair in Aquila. Zhinü came down to Earth and, while bathing in a river, met Niulang; he stole her clothes, and unable to return to heaven without them she decided to marry him. When the heavenly queen found out about their union she tore them apart, condemning them to live on opposite sides of the Milky Way. Qixi is celebrated on the seventh night of the seventh lunar month, when a bridge of magpies forms across the sky for the lovers to cross. Yue Xia Laoren, the old lunar matchmaker god, is the Taoist deity in charge of the red thread and of marriages, typically represented with a staff in his right hand, a marital register in his left, and red thread draped over his arms.

Yue Xia Laoren, the old lunar matchmaker god, is the Taoist deity in charge of the red thread and of marriages, typically represented with a staff in his right hand, a marital register in his left, and red thread draped over his arms.

claims.notes: Quartigod son of Arjuna (Indra-paternal demigod) by Subhadrā (Krishna's sister). The Chakravyuha-breach death on day 13 of the Kurukshetra war is one of the most-cited tragic-injustice episodes in the entire Hindu tradition: the in-utero-learning of the entry-pattern but not the exit, the day-13 isolation when his fellow Pandavas were stopped at the gate by Jayadratha's Shiva-boon, the dharma-yuddha violation by six simultaneous attackers, and the resulting Arjuna pratijñā that drove the Jayadratha-vadha on day 14. Father of Parikshit by Uttarā — through Parikshit, ancestor of Janamejaya at whose snake-sacrifice the Mahābhārata is canonically narrated by Vaiśampāyana, making Abhimanyu the structural-genealogical hinge between the war-narrative and the frame-narrative of the epic itself.

lifecycle.notes: On day 13 of the Kurukshetra war, with Arjuna drawn away to the southern flank by the Trigarta-Samshaptaka army, Drona arranged the Kaurava forces in the Chakravyuha. Abhimanyu was the only Pandava-side warrior who knew how to enter — but not how to exit. Yudhishthira ordered him to lead the breach with the four other Pandavas following to support him. The Pandavas were stopped at the entry by Jayadratha's Shiva-boon power; Abhimanyu was trapped alone inside.

lifecycle.notes: Killed inside the Chakravyuha by six Kaurava warriors attacking him simultaneously — a violation of the dharma-yuddha (righteous-warfare) code that mandated single-combat. Drona, Karṇa, Kṛpa, Aśvatthāmā, Bṛhadbala, and Kṛtavarmā together overwhelmed him after his chariot was disabled, his bow broken, and his sword shattered. The death triggered Arjuna's pratijñā (vow) to kill Jayadratha by sunset of the following day, the central drama of Mahabharata day 14. The "Abhimanyu-vadha" (death of Abhimanyu) episode is one of the most-cited tragic-injustice narratives in the entire Hindu tradition.

citations.reference: Mahabharata Adi Parva 102-103 (the kidnapping); Udyoga Parva 170-194 (the Amba narrative — twelve-year penance, Parashurama-Bhishma duel, self-immolation, rebirth as Shikhandini, yaksha exchange); Bhishma Parva 107-119 (the tenth day, Bhishma's fall); Sauptika Parva 8 (death by Ashvatthama)

claims.notes: Eldest of three Kashi princesses (Amba, Ambika, Ambalika); kidnapped by Bhishma at the svayamvara as a wife for Vichitravirya. Revealed her prior love for Salwa, king of Saubha; Bhishma honorably released her; but Salwa rejected her as defiled by abduction, and Vichitravirya rejected her likewise. Returned to Bhishma demanding marriage; Bhishma's vow forbade; sent away. Sought revenge through Parashurama, who fought Bhishma in a 23-day stalemate-duel on her behalf and lost. Undertook twelve years of severe ascetic penance; pleased Shiva, who granted her the boon of becoming the cause of Bhishma's death in her next birth (since Bhishma's vow forbade fighting a woman). Self-immolated to enable the rebirth. Reborn as Shikhandini, daughter of King Drupada of Panchala (the same king whose later sacrifice produced Draupadi and Dhrishtadyumna). Drupada raised her as a male per Shiva's prophecy. After her marriage to a princess of Dasharna led to the discovery of her female sex and threatened war, fled to the forest and exchanged sexes with the yaksha Sthuna; the exchange became permanent when Kubera cursed the yaksha to retain the female sex. On the tenth day of Kurukshetra, placed before Arjuna in the chariot to nullify Bhishma's vow against fighting one born female; Bhishma recognized Shikhandi as reborn Amba and lowered his bow; Arjuna shot from behind, pinning Bhishma to the bed of arrows. The Shiva-boon fulfilled. Killed by Ashvatthama on the eighteenth night during the sleeping-camp massacre.

Greatest archer of the epic; recipient of the Bhagavad Gītā discourse from Krishna at Kurukshetra (Bhīṣma Parva 23-40), which became the central philosophical text of Hindu religious tradition. Wins Draupadī at her svayamvara disguised as a brahmin. Wields the Gāṇḍīva bow (Agni's gift at Khāṇḍava). Receives the Pāśupatāstra from Shiva after the kirāta-combat austerities. Kills Karṇa not knowing they are full brothers by Kuntī — the structural-tragic core of the epic. Falls in the great-departure march; karmic fault: pride in his archery.

claims.notes: Quartigod son of Arjuna (Indra-paternal demigod) by Citrāṅgadā of Maṇipūra. King of Maṇipūra by maternal-grandfather succession per the marriage-stipulation that excluded Citrāṅgadā's sons from the Kuru inheritance. The patricide-then-revival episode in Āśvamedhika Parva 79-81 — Babhruvāhana killing Arjuna during the Aśvamedha horse-pursuit, then Ulūpī (his stepmother, Iravan's mother) reviving Arjuna with the saṃjīvana-maṇi — is one of the canonical structural-tragic episodes of the Mahābhārata, paralleling Cú Chulainn × Connla, Rustam × Sohrab, and the broader Indo-European patricidal pattern.

Citrāṅgadā's father stipulated that any son born would inherit Maṇipūra rather than join the Kuru lineage — making Babhruvāhana the kingdom-of-Maṇipūra heir rather than a Hastināpura claimant. Quartigod-tier (1/4 divine through paternal Indra-line).

The patricide is one of the canonical structural-tragic Mahābhārata episodes (parallel to Cú Chulainn's killing of Connla in the Irish tradition, Sohrab and Rustam in the Persian tradition, and the Oedipal pattern across multiple Indo-European corpora). Ulūpī (Iravan's mother, also Arjuna's wife and now stepmother to Babhruvāhana) revived Arjuna with the saṃjīvana-maṇi (life-restoring nāga jewel).

linguistic.etymology: Sanskrit बभ्रुवाहन (Babhruvāhana), from babhru "tawny, reddish-brown" and vāhana "mount, vehicle," "he of the tawny mount" — son of Arjuna and Citrāṅgadā, king of Maṇipūra.

variants.notes: The karmic-incarnation reading: Bhishma is the Vasu Dyaus, chief of the eight Vasus, condemned by Vasishtha's curse for his role in stealing the wish-fulfilling cow Nandini at his wife's request. The seven other Vasus were drowned by Ganga at birth and immediately released; Dyaus, as the most culpable, was condemned to a long mortal life — Bhishma's entire 200-year-plus lifespan and accumulated grief is the karmic working-out of that curse. The strict-criterion classification under the registry follows the textual surface (Ganga + Shantanu biological parentage) with the Vasu-incarnation karmic-soul-history layer recorded as variant — structurally parallel to Mongán-pattern (medieval-literary divine-paternity reading), to Bhīma's Vāyu-incarnation framing, and to the Šulgi case (Ur III royal-hymn divine-paternity claim).

claims.notes: Demigod son of the river-goddess Ganga by the mortal Kuru king Shantanu of Hastinapura; one of the most fully developed characters in the Mahabharata and a continuing major figure in Hindu religious-cultural memory. Birth name Devavrata; received the name Bhīṣma ("of the terrible vow") after his double-vow of renunciation of the throne and lifelong celibacy, taken to enable his father Shantanu's second marriage to Satyavati. In gratitude Shantanu granted him icchamrityu — death-at-will. Educated by Vasishtha, Brihaspati, Shukra, and Parashurama. Kidnapped Amba, Ambika, and Ambalika of Kashi for Vichitravirya's marriage; Amba's rejection-rage produced her decades-long ascetic rebirth as Shikhandi, the eventual instrument of Bhishma's fall. Fought Parashurama in a twenty-three-day stalemate-duel. Served as regent of Hastinapura through the entire Pandava-Kaurava generation; bound by his vow of service to the throne, fought as commander of the Kaurava forces for the first ten days of the Kurukshetra war despite his moral preference for the Pandavas. Fell on the tenth day to Arjuna with Shikhandi placed before him (Bhishma's vow forbade fighting one born female). Lay 58 days on the bed of arrows (shara-shayya); chose through icchamrityu to wait for uttarayana (winter solstice) before releasing his prana; in those 58 days delivered the deathbed instruction to Yudhishthira on rajadharma, apaddharma, and moksha-dharma — the Shanti Parva and Anushasana Parva, the longest pedagogical sequence of the Mahabharata at c. 35,000+ verses, foundational text for Hindu political theory and dharma. Includes the Vishnu Sahasranama, the thousand names of Vishnu, recited in continuing daily Hindu practice. The Bhishmashtami observance (eighth day of the bright half of Magha) commemorates his death on uttarayana with tarpana water-offerings for ancestors. The strict-criterion classification follows the textual surface (Ganga + Shantanu biological parentage) with the Vasu-Dyaus karmic-incarnation reading recorded in variants[] — structurally parallel to the Mongán medieval-literary divine-paternity case, to Bhīma's Vāyu-incarnation framing, and to the Šulgi Ur III royal-hymn case.

lifecycle.notes: Educated by Vasishtha (Vedas, dharma-shastras), Brihaspati (statecraft and rhetoric), Shukra (politics), Parashurama (military arts and astra-weapons). Returned to Hastinapura aged sixteen; Shantanu installed him as crown prince (yuvaraja).

sources.reference: Mahabharata Adi Parva 100

lifecycle.notes: When Shantanu wished to marry Satyavati and her father (the chief of the fisher-folk) demanded that Satyavati's son inherit the throne, Devavrata went to the fisher-chief and took the bhīṣma double-vow: renunciation of the throne (no descendant of his could ever displace Satyavati's sons) and lifelong celibacy (no descendants of his at all). The terrified gods showered flowers from heaven and called him "Bhīṣma" — "of the terrible vow." The double-vow renounced both kingship and offspring, the two foundational kshatriya goods.

sources.reference: Mahabharata Adi Parva 100

lifecycle.notes: Shantanu in gratitude granted Devavrata icchamrityu — death-at-will. Bhishma could not be killed against his consent; he would die only when he himself chose to release his prana. The boon would later allow him to lie 58 days on the bed of arrows after his fall on the tenth day of the Mahabharata war, waiting for the auspicious moment of uttarayana (winter solstice) to release his life.

sources.reference: Mahabharata Adi Parva 102; Udyoga Parva 170-194 (the Amba narrative)

lifecycle.notes: When Vichitravirya came of age, Bhishma kidnapped the three daughters (Amba, Ambika, Ambalika) of the king of Kashi from their svayamvara to be Vichitravirya's wives — the kshatriya marriage-by-abduction, dharmic for warrior-class. Amba revealed she had already chosen Salwa as her husband at the svayamvara; Bhishma sent her back; Salwa rejected her as no longer his (having been touched by another man); Amba returned and demanded Bhishma marry her. Bhishma's vow forbade it. Amba's rage at this rejection became her life's purpose.

sources.reference: Mahabharata Udyoga Parva 178-188

lifecycle.notes: Amba sought Parashurama (Bhishma's former teacher) as her champion. Parashurama, bound by guru-duty to her, challenged Bhishma. Twenty-three-day duel of astra-weapons; ended in stalemate when the divine seers commanded peace. Parashurama acknowledged that he could not defeat Bhishma; Amba turned to direct ascetic penance.

sources.reference: Mahabharata Adi Parva 102-104

lifecycle.notes: After Vichitravirya's death without children, Bhishma refused Satyavati's repeated requests that he break his vow to father heirs. Instead Vyasa (Satyavati's premarital son by sage Parashara) was called to perform niyoga on Vichitravirya's widows Ambika and Ambalika (producing Dhritarashtra and Pandu) and on a maidservant (producing Vidura). Bhishma served as regent and grand-uncle through the entire Pandava-Kaurava generation.

sources.reference: Mahabharata Adi Parva 130-141

lifecycle.notes: Oversaw the education of the Pandavas and Kauravas under Drona and Kripa. Throughout the dice-game humiliation of Draupadi and the events leading to the war, Bhishma counseled compromise but ultimately remained bound by his vow of service to the throne of Hastinapura — meaning the Kauravas, despite his moral disagreement.

sources.reference: Mahabharata Bhishma Parva (Books 6) 1-117

lifecycle.notes: Commander of the eleven Kaurava akshauhinis for the first ten days of the Kurukshetra war. The Bhagavad Gita (Bhishma Parva 23-40) is recited by Krishna to Arjuna at the moment Arjuna saw Bhishma in the enemy line and froze with grief. Bhishma fought on the Kaurava side bound by his vow of service to the throne, but with the explicit caveat to Yudhishthira on the eve of war: "I am bound to fight for Duryodhana but I will not be the cause of your defeat. Come to me before any battle and I will tell you the means of my own fall." On the ninth night, Yudhishthira and the Pandavas did exactly this; Bhishma told them his fall would come through Shikhandi (Amba reborn), against whom he would not raise weapons because Shikhandi had been born female (as Shikhandini, daughter of Drupada).

sources.reference: Mahabharata Bhishma Parva 117-119

lifecycle.notes: On the tenth day, Arjuna with Shikhandi placed before him (so that Bhishma's vow forbade him to fire) shot Bhishma down with arrow after arrow. Bhishma fell from his chariot and lay supported above the ground by the arrows piercing him — the famous shara-shayya, the bed of arrows. Did not die: invoking icchamrityu, he chose to wait for uttarayana (the winter solstice, the auspicious northern path of the sun) before releasing his prana.

sources.reference: Mahabharata Shanti Parva (Books 12) 1-353; Anushasana Parva (Book 13) 1-167

lifecycle.notes: Lay 58 days on the bed of arrows. After the Kaurava defeat, Yudhishthira came to him for instruction. The Shanti Parva and Anushasana Parva (together one of the longest pedagogical sequences in any world epic, c. 35,000+ verses) are Bhishma's deathbed teaching to Yudhishthira on rajadharma (royal duty), apaddharma (duty in extremity), moksha-dharma (liberation), and the systematic exposition of dharma. Includes the Vishnu Sahasranama (the thousand names of Vishnu, recited in continuing Hindu daily practice).

sources.reference: Mahabharata Anushasana Parva 167-168

lifecycle.notes: On the day of uttarayana — the winter solstice and the start of the auspicious northern-path-of-the-sun — Bhishma released his prana through the crown of his head in yogic meditation, returning to his Vasu-Dyaus status. Pandavas and Krishna performed his last rites at the Ganga.

claims.notes: Born from the sacrificial fire (yajna-kunda) of King Drupada of Panchala, fully grown, alongside her brother Dhrishtadyumna. The yajna was performed by Yaja and Upayaja for Drupada's vengeance on Drona; Dhrishtadyumna emerged as the fated killer of Drona, Draupadi as the fated wife of the Pandavas and instrument of the Kuru destruction. Won by Arjuna at her svayamvara via the rotating-fish-eye archery test; became the shared wife of all five Pandavas through Kunti's blind-instruction ("share equally"). The disrobing in court by Dushasana after Yudhishthira lost the dice-game — Krishna's miraculous extension of her sari — is the single most-depicted scene of the Mahabharata in continuing Hindu visual culture; her vow not to tie her hair until washed in Dushasana's blood structurally caused the Kurukshetra war. Twelve years of forest exile with the Pandavas; thirteenth year incognito at Virata's court as Sairandhri. Lost all five sons (the Upapandavas) to Ashvatthama's sleeping-camp night massacre after the war's eighteenth day. Died on the mountainside during the mahaprasthana final journey toward Mt. Meru — the first of the six (five Pandavas plus Draupadi) to fall, identified by Yudhishthira as having loved Arjuna more than the other four. The Lakshmi-incarnation reading (recorded in variants[]) is the major Puranic-bhakti theological reading of her place in the cosmic order; strict-criterion classification stays at mortal.

lifecycle.notes: After Yudhishthira lost the dice-game at Hastinapura (staking Draupadi as a wager after losing himself), Dushasana dragged her by the hair into the assembly during her menstruation period; attempted to disrobe her in court. Krishna's miraculous extension of her sari (becoming infinitely long as Dushasana pulled, exhausting him) is the most-depicted single scene of the Mahabharata in continuing Hindu visual culture. The vow she made during this humiliation (not to tie her hair until it was washed in Dushasana's blood) is the structural cause of the war-vows by Bhima (to break Duryodhana's thigh and tear out Dushasana's heart) that drove the Kurukshetra war.

claims.notes: Hindu river-goddess; personification of the Ganges river. The most worshipped river-deity in Hinduism and arguably the most actively cultivated continuing female deity in any world religion (the daily Ganga Aarti at Varanasi has run continuously for centuries). First attested in the Rigveda (Nadistuti hymn, 10.75 — c. 1500-1200 BCE) where she is named in the standard list of seven sacred rivers. Iconographically standardized by the Gupta period riding her makara-vahana (crocodilian water-creature mount), holding a kalasha (water-pot). Mythological narrative-cycle: descended from heaven through the matted locks of Shiva to the Himalayas in response to Bhagiratha's thousand-year austerities, purifying the ashes of his ancestor Sagara's 60,000 sons (Ramayana Bala Kanda 42-44). Married Shantanu, mortal Kuru king of Hastinapura, under condition of unquestioning acceptance; bore him eight sons — the eight Vasus reborn through Vasishtha's curse for stealing his wish-fulfilling cow Nandini; drowned the first seven at birth in the Ganga to release them from their cursed mortal incarnations; on the eighth Shantanu intervened, breaking the condition; Ganga revealed the curse, returned the boy (Devavrata, later Bhishma — the Vasu Dyaus, chief of the eight and the most culpable, condemned to a long mortal life) to Shantanu when grown, and departed (Mahabharata Adi Parva 91-100). Foster-mother of Karttikeya/Skanda when Agni cast Shiva's seed upon her. Continuing major cult — Gangotri (the source), Haridwar (the plains-descent), Varanasi (Manikarnika cremation ghat), Allahabad/Prayagraj (Triveni Sangam — site of the 2025 Maha Kumbha Mela that drew over 600 million pilgrims, the largest single religious gathering in human history), Sagar Island (the mouth). Bathing in Ganga purifies all sins; death on her banks confers moksha. The Ganga is also a continuing object of major environmental and political contention as the most heavily polluted of the world's great sacred rivers.

claims.notes: Quartigod son of Bhīma (Vāyu-paternal demigod) by the rākṣasī Hiḍimbā. Born already a young man via the accelerated-rākṣasa-pregnancy pattern. The canonical loyal-non-Aryan-allied-warrior of the Mahābhārata: a rākṣasa by maternal blood, but devoted to his Pāṇḍava paternal-kin from birth. The death by Karṇa's Vāsava-Śakti on the night of day 14 of Kurukshetra is one of the most-cited Krishna-strategic-instigations in the war-narrative — Krishna deliberately drove Ghaṭotkaca to attack so that Karṇa would expend the Indra-given spear that had been reserved for Arjuna, the trade made openly: Ghaṭotkaca's life for Arjuna's. The dying-fall of his giant-form crushing thousands of Kaurava soldiers makes his death even-in-defeat one of the highest tactical contributions of the war.

lifecycle.notes: Killed on the night of day 14 of the Kurukshetra war by Karṇa's Vāsava-Śakti (the divine spear that Indra had given Karṇa in exchange for his kavaca-and-kuṇḍala). The structural-tactical significance: Karṇa had reserved the Vāsava-Śakti specifically for Arjuna, but was forced to expend it on Ghaṭotkaca to halt the rākṣasa's night-attack devastation of the Kaurava army — Krishna had specifically instigated the Ghaṭotkaca-attack to compel Karṇa to use the spear on the secondary target. Ghaṭotkaca's dying-act was to fall in his giant-form onto the Kaurava soldiers below, killing thousands more in the death-fall. Krishna celebrated the death openly: "now Arjuna will live."

linguistic.etymology: Sanskrit इन्द्र (Indra) is of contested but inherited Indo-Iranian origin (cf. the Avestan demon Indra and the Mitanni treaty god in-da-ra, c. 1380 BCE). Mayrhofer leaves the ultimate root uncertain; among proposals are a connection to indu- "drop, soma" or to a base conveying "force, strength, virility" (whence indriya- "power, sense-faculty"). Yāska's Nirukta (10.8) offers folk-etymologies linking the name to verbs of giving and irradiating. The name is pan-Vedic and addressed in roughly a quarter of the Ṛgveda.

claims.notes: Scion-tier (registry-floor) descendant of Arjuna — through Arjuna → Abhimanyu → Parīkṣit → Janamejaya — making him the structural-narrative-frame audience of the entire Mahābhārata. Vyāsa's disciple Vaiśampāyana recites the epic to Janamejaya during the sarpasattra (snake-sacrifice) at Takṣaśīlā that Janamejaya conducts to avenge his father's death by Takṣaka. The narration-during-sacrifice establishes the canonical recursive frame: the war-epic exists as told to the great-grandson of the demigod war-hero, in the Kuru-court of the early kali-yuga, recorded by the sage Vyāsa who is also a character within the war-narrative he composed. Janamejaya Pārikṣita is also independently attested in the older Brahmanic tradition (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 8.21, Atharvaveda-pariśiṣṭa) as a Vedic ritual-king — making him the cross-corpus link between the post-Vedic ritualized-court tradition and the epic-frame tradition.

lifecycle.notes: Conducted the sarpasattra (snake-sacrifice) at Takṣaśīlā to avenge his father's death — the great rite intended to incinerate every snake on earth. Halted by the brahmin Āstīka (whose mother Jaratkārū was the sister of the snake-king Vāsuki) who invoked the Indra-vow that protected Takṣaka from the fire-sacrifice. Vyāsa's disciple Vaiśampāyana narrates the entire Mahābhārata to Janamejaya during the sarpasattra — making Janamejaya the canonical narrative-frame audience of the epic itself, the structural pivot that contains the war-narrative within the post-war Kuru continuation.

linguistic.etymology: Sanskrit जनमेजय (Janamejaya), from jana "men, people" and the causative mejaya "causing to tremble" (√ji/ej), "he who makes men tremble" — the Kuru king whose snake-sacrifice frames the recitation of the Mahābhārata.

claims.notes: This is lane 14's five-of-six pattern in its worst form. Dasharatha has three queens. The corpus held Kausalya and Sumitra — the mothers of Rama and of Lakshmana, that is, the two whose sons are already in the registry — and not Kaikeyi, whose act is the reason there is a story. A corpus that adds people because other people it holds are related to them will always produce this shape, and it is worth naming as a mechanism rather than as a run of bad luck.

sources.reference: Reference treatment: Manthara, Kaikeyi's maid, poisoned Kaikeyi's mind with the idea that the throne rightfully belonged to her son Bharata and not to Rama; Kaikeyi asked for two boons — first, that Bharata should be crowned as king, and second, that Rama should be sent on exile for fourteen years; the fourteen-year exile ensured that Rama would be away long enough for Bharata to firmly establish his rule in Ayodhya.

lifecycle.startEvent: It does not work. Bharata is appalled by his mother and refuses the throne, ruling Ayodhya as Rama's representative until Rama comes back.

claims.notes: The structural-tragic hero of the Mahabharata; demigod son of Sūrya by Kuntī in girlhood, pre-marriage. Born clad in the kavacha (divine armor) and kuṇḍala (earrings) — Sūrya's paternal gifts conferring invulnerability. Abandoned by Kuntī in shame; raised by the Sūta charioteer Adhiratha and his wife Rādhā as Vasuṣeṇa. Cursed twice — by Paraśurāma (whose tutelage he obtained by claiming to be a brahmin: the Brahmāstra-mantra will fail him at his moment of greatest need) and by a brahmin whose cow he accidentally killed (his chariot wheel will sink into the earth in his decisive battle). Surrenders the kavacha and kuṇḍala to Indra disguised as a brahmin (Vana Parva 308) — supreme dāna at the cost of his life. Receives the Vāsavī Śakti in return; spends it on Ghaṭotkaca on Krishna's strategic compulsion. Discovers his true parentage from Kuntī on the eve of Kurukshetra (Udyoga Parva 144); promises her she will retain five sons either way. Killed by Arjuna on day seventeen when both curses converge — wheel sunk, mantra failed — and Krishna counsels Arjuna to strike against the rules of combat. Yudhiṣṭhira learns of the brotherhood only afterward; the discovery devastates him. The Karṇa Parva (Book 8) is wholly devoted to him.

linguistic.etymology: Sanskrit लक्ष्मी (lakṣmī́) originally meant "mark, sign, token (of fortune), good luck," from the root lakṣ- "to mark, perceive" (related to lakṣaṇa "mark"); the sense narrowed to "good fortune" and was personified as the goddess of prosperity. Mayrhofer treats lakṣmī́- under lakṣ-, noting the Ṛgvedic neutral sense "mark/sign" (RV 10.71.2) which only later specialized as auspicious. Her epithet श्री (Śrī) "splendor, prosperity" is a separate inherited word.

claims.notes: Eldest of the five Upapāṇḍavas (the sons of Draupadī by the five Pāṇḍavas, one by each husband). Quartigod-tier through paternal Dharma-line via Yudhiṣṭhira. Killed in the Sauptika-massacre on the night after the Kurukshetra war — Aśvatthāmā, mistaking the sleeping Upapāṇḍavas for their Pāṇḍava fathers, slaughtered all five along with Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Śikhaṇḍī. The collective death of the Upapāṇḍavas terminates the dynastic continuation of the Pāṇḍava-line through Draupadī, leaving only Abhimanyu's posthumously-revived son Parīkṣit (through Subhadrā's line) to continue the Kuru dynasty.

sources.reference: Mahābhārata Ādi Parva 95.75, 220 (BORI Critical Edition)

lifecycle.notes: Eldest of the five Upapāṇḍavas (sons of Draupadī by the five Pāṇḍavas — one by each husband during the rotational-marriage period). Son of Yudhiṣṭhira (Dharma-paternal demigod) by Draupadī. Quartigod-tier (1/4 divine through paternal Dharma-line).

sources.reference: Mahābhārata Ādi Parva 220-221

lifecycle.notes: Trained at Indraprastha alongside his four half-brothers and the other Pandava-court princes; reached martial maturity by the time of the Kurukshetra war.

sources.reference: Mahābhārata Sauptika Parva 8.50-65

lifecycle.notes: Killed in his sleep on the night after the Kurukshetra war ended — Aśvatthāmā, in his Rudra-empowered night-raid avenging Duryodhana, entered the Pāṇḍava camp and slaughtered the five Upapāṇḍavas (mistaken for the five Pāṇḍavas themselves), Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍī, and the remaining Pāñcāla forces. The Sauptika-massacre is the structural turning-point that makes the Pāṇḍava victory pyrrhic; the Stri Parva grief-cycle is dominated by Draupadī's mourning for her five sons.

linguistic.etymology: Sanskrit प्रतिविन्ध्य (Prativindhya), from prati "facing, towards" and Vindhya (the Vindhya range), "facing the Vindhya" — said to be born facing those mountains; eldest of the Upapāṇḍavas, son of Yudhiṣṭhira and Draupadī.

claims.notes: Foundational Mahabharata mortal-figure; mother of Vyasa (the redactor of the Mahabharata), Chitrangada, and Vichitravirya. Born to King Vasu Uparichara of Chedi by the apsara Adrika (transformed into a fish by curse) — twin parturition giving the male twin to Vasu and the female twin (Satyavati) to Dasharaja, the chief of the fisher-folk. Hence her epithet Matsyagandhā ("the Fish-Scented"). While ferrying the sage Parashara across the Yamuna, agreed to sexual union in exchange for boons. Bore Vyasa immediately; he grew to adulthood at once and departed for ascetic practice. Married Shantanu after Devavrata's bhīṣma-vow; bore Chitrangada and Vichitravirya. After both sons died without heirs, summoned Vyasa to perform niyoga on Vichitravirya's widows Ambika and Ambalika, producing Dhritarashtra (blind because Ambika closed her eyes at Vyasa's terrifying ascetic appearance), Pandu (pale because Ambalika paled), and Vidura (by a substituted maidservant). The niyoga-substitution mechanism is the structural origin of the Pandava-Kaurava generation. Retired to the forest with her daughters-in-law before the Kurukshetra war; died as an ascetic. The Mahabharata's entire compositional framing (Vyasa narrating to Vaishampayana to Janamejaya at the snake-sacrifice) traces back to Satyavati through her premarital union with Parashara.

claims.notes: TYPE CORRECTED UNDER TEST, and this is the SECOND lane running in which the same thing happened. The treatment says 'Shani is a demi-god' in as many words, and the record was authored that way. npm test rejected it as tier-classification drift: this corpus computes the tier from DESCENT, and both his parents — Surya and a woman made of shadow — are deities in the corpus, so the pipeline computes 'deity'. Lane 16 hit the identical problem from the other direction with Ashwatthama, authored 'demigod' against a computed 'mortal'. The finding is worth stating once: THE SOURCE'S WORD AND THE CORPUS'S COMPUTED TIER ARE DIFFERENT KINDS OF CLAIM. A treatment saying 'demi-god' is describing status; this schema's tier is a function of parentage. Where they disagree the schema wins, because the alternative is a corpus whose type field means two things. He is the most propitiated of the nine in living practice, and the one most people arrange their week around; the corpus held the sun who fathered him and not him.

claims.notes: Mortal Kuru king of Hastinapura; father of Bhishma (by Ganga) and Chitrangada and Vichitravirya (by Satyavati). Met the river-goddess Ganga in the form of a beautiful woman on the banks of the Ganges; married her under the condition of unquestioning acceptance. Bore eight sons by her; she drowned the first seven at birth (the Vasu-curse release); on the eighth Shantanu intervened, breaking the condition; lost Ganga, who took the boy (Devavrata) with her. Reunited with the grown Devavrata sixteen years later. Years later, his desire to marry the fisher-woman Satyavati prompted Devavrata's bhīṣma-vow of renunciation and celibacy — for which Shantanu granted Devavrata the boon of icchamrityu (death-at-will). Bore Chitrangada and Vichitravirya by Satyavati but died before either could rule effectively. Forms the structural foundation of the Mahabharata's Kuru-dynastic crisis: his second-marriage compromise produces Bhishma's vow, which produces the throne-succession problem (no Bhishma descendants), which produces the niyoga-conception of Dhritarashtra and Pandu by Vyasa on the widows of Vichitravirya, which produces the Pandava-Kaurava rivalry that culminates in the Kurukshetra war.

lifecycle.notes: Met Ganga on the riverbank of the Ganges in the form of a beautiful woman. She agreed to marry him under the condition that he never question her actions and never restrain her. Bore him eight sons; she drowned the first seven at birth.

lifecycle.notes: On the eighth child, Shantanu intervened — could not bear another infanticide. Ganga revealed the Vasu-curse (the eight Vasus had stolen Vasishtha's wish-fulfilling cow Nandini at the request of Dyaus's wife; Vasishtha cursed them to be born mortal; the seven were released at birth; Dyaus, the chief instigator, was condemned to a long mortal life as the eighth). She departed, taking the eighth (Devavrata) with her.

sources.reference: Mahabharata Adi Parva 100

lifecycle.notes: Sixteen years later, Shantanu met a young man arresting the flow of the Ganga with arrows; Ganga emerged and revealed him as Devavrata, returned to his father grown and educated. Shantanu installed Devavrata as crown prince (yuvaraja).

sources.reference: Mahabharata Adi Parva 100-101

lifecycle.notes: Years later met Satyavati, the fisher-woman who ferried travelers across the Yamuna. Asked her father (the chief of the fisher-folk) for her in marriage; the father demanded that her son inherit the throne, displacing Devavrata. Shantanu refused. Devavrata, learning of his father's grief, went himself to the fisher-chief and took the bhīṣma ("terrible") double-vow: he renounced the throne and took lifelong celibacy, ensuring no descendants of his could ever challenge Satyavati's sons. The terrified gods showered flowers; Shantanu in gratitude granted Devavrata the boon of icchamrityu (death-at-will). From that day Devavrata was called Bhishma.

linguistic.etymology: Sanskrit शिव (śiva) is originally an adjective meaning "auspicious, kind, gracious, benign," used euphemistically of the fierce Vedic Rudra (the "Howler") before crystallizing as the proper name of the god. Mayrhofer connects śiva- to a PIE root *ḱey- "to be dear, lie/settle," cognate with the family of Latin cīvis and the notion of "the friendly/familiar one"; the euphemistic use parallels Greek Eumenides. The Śatarudrīya (Yajurveda) already applies śiva to Rudra as a propitiatory epithet.

claims.notes: Yamī, the twin sister of Yama and, as the deified river Yamunā (Kālindī), a daughter of the Sun. Authored as ONE figure because the corpus uses 'Yamī/Yamunā' for a single person (cf. hindu_yama notes 'twin of Yami'; the Bhāī Dūj gloss 'his sister Yamī/Yamunā'). Child of Sūrya (parentId hindu_surya, father); her mother is Saraṇyū (Purāṇic Saṃjñā/Chāyā), who has no registered figure and so is named here rather than placed in parentIds. Typed demigod by the mandated descent rule (Sūrya deity 1.0 + unregistered mother 0.0, /2 = 0.5 → demigod; the drift-safe lower tier). claims.notes: Eldest Pandava; demigod son of Dharma by Kuntī. Embodiment of dharma — his truthfulness is so absolute that his chariot was said to hover above the ground; the single half-truth he utters (about Aśvatthāmā's death, Drona Parva 191) causes it to touch earth for the first time. King of Indraprastha after the Pandava settlement, then of Hastināpura after Kurukshetra. Loses everything to Śakuni's loaded dice in the gambling hall (Sabha Parva), triggering the thirteen-year exile and ultimately the war. Only Pandava to ascend to heaven in his physical body (Svargārohaṇa Parva); refuses to enter without his dog (revealed as Dharma in disguise — his father testing him one final time).

linguistic.etymology: Japanese 天照大御神 / アマテラス Amaterasu, from Old Japanese ama 'heaven, sky' (天) + terasu 'to shine on, illuminate' (照らす), the transitive/causative of teru 'to shine' (照る) — 'she who shines in / illuminates heaven.' The full title Amaterasu-Ōmikami adds oho 'great' (大) + mi- honorific (御) + kami 'deity' (神). Her alternate name Ōhirume (大日孁) contains hiru < hi 'sun' (日) + me 'woman.' The solar etymology is transparent and attested from the Kojiki (712) and Nihon Shoki (720).

linguistic.etymology: Japanese 弁才天 / 弁財天 Benzaiten is a Buddhist loan-rendering of Sanskrit सरस्वती Sarasvatī, the river-goddess of speech and learning, who in the Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra (Konkōmyōkyō 金光明経) is styled Sarasvatī-devī. Chinese translators rendered her name partly by sense: 辯才天 biàncái-tiān 'deva of eloquence/debating-talent' (辯/弁 biàn 'eloquence, debate' + 才 cái 'talent') + 天 tiān 'deva, heaven(ly being).' The variant 弁財天 substitutes 財 'wealth' (homophone zai), reflecting her later association with riches. Japanese reads the characters Ben-zai-ten. The source-name Sarasvatī itself means 'she of the pool/flowing waters,' from saras 'lake, pool' + possessive -vatī.

linguistic.etymology: Japanese 恵比須 / 蛭子 Ebisu. The name derives from Old Japanese ye-bisu / emishi (夷/戎), a word meaning 'foreigner, easterner, barbarian, stranger from beyond,' applied to peoples and beings coming from outside (the same root underlies Emishi, the eastern peoples). The fishing-luck god is 'the visitor from across the sea,' a stranger-deity washing ashore — hence the identification with Hiruko (蛭子 'leech-child'), the cast-away first child of Izanagi and Izanami, the name 蛭子 also being read Ebisu. The auspicious spelling 恵比須/恵比寿 ('blessing-compare-must/longevity') is phonetic ateji.

linguistic.etymology: Japanese 伊邪那岐 Izanagi-no-Mikoto (man'yōgana, phonetic). The standard derivation takes the stem from Old Japanese izana(p)u 'to invite, beckon, allure' (誘う), since in the Kojiki the pair invite one another to wed; the final -gi/-ki is the Old Japanese masculine name-element (ki 'male,' contrasting with -mi 'female' in Izanami). The name is thus 'the inviting male (deity).' The phonetic kanji 伊邪那岐 carry no independent meaning.

The 660 BC date is a seventh-century back-calculation — a grand cycle of 1,260 years counted back from a year the compilers cared about — and is recorded as what the chronicles say rather than as when anything happened.

linguistic.etymology: 火之迦具土神 Hi-no-Kagutsuchi, the fire-kami whose birth scalded Izanami to death. The name combines kagu — connected to Old Japanese kagu/kago 'to glow, flicker, shine' (the same element underlying kagayaku 'to shine, blaze') — + tsuchi (土/槌), an Old Japanese suffix forming names of spirits and serpentine/numinous beings (cf. Ōrochi's element, and the spirit-suffix -tsuchi/-zuchi as in Nozuchi). The prefix Hi-no- is hi 'fire' (火). The whole names 'the glowing/blazing spirit (of fire).' The characters 迦具土 are phonographic man'yōgana for kagutsuchi.

linguistic.etymology: 木花之佐久夜毘売 Ko-no-hana-no-Sakuya-hime, the blossom-princess and wife of Ninigi. The name is transparent Old Japanese: ko-no-hana 'the blossom(s) of the tree(s)' (木 ko 'tree' + no genitive + 花 hana 'flower/blossom') + sakuya, from saku 'to bloom, blossom' (咲く) + an exclamatory/emphatic -ya — 'the blossoms that bloom!' + hime 'princess, noble lady' (毘売, OJ pime, pi 'sun/noble' + me 'woman'). Thus 'Princess of the Blooming Tree-blossoms,' a name evoking the transient flowering she personifies (and, in the myth, the brevity of life). The characters 佐久夜毘売 are phonographic.

claims.notes: He agrees immediately and then removes himself, which is the least examined and most consequential act in the episode: Izumo's case is conceded by the son whose office is speaking on his father's behalf, and then the spokesman is gone. His disappearance is described as hiding himself behind a green fence of branches, which is the formula the Kojiki uses for a god withdrawing from the world. He is widely identified with Ebisu, whom the registry already holds, and the census records that identification without merging the two.

linguistic.etymology: 邇邇芸命 Ninigi-no-Mikoto (full name Ame-nigishi-kuni-nigishi-amatsuhiko-hiko-ho-no-ninigi-no-Mikoto). The reduplicated element nigi/nigishi reflects Old Japanese nik(i)/nigi 'soft, calm, abundant, luxuriant' (cf. nigi-mitama 'gentle spirit'), and in the long name pairs ame-nigishi 'heaven-abounding' with kuni-nigishi 'land-abounding.' The core ho-no-ninigi has ho 'ear/head of grain, ripe rice' (穂) — so the name evokes the lush ripening of grain (nigi-nigishi 'abundantly flourishing'), fitting the heavenly grandson who descends to rule the rice-land. The kanji 邇邇芸 are phonographic.

linguistic.etymology: 大国主神 Ōkuninushi-no-Kami, transparently ō (OJ opo) 'great' (大) + kuni 'land, country, province' (国) + nushi 'master, lord, owner' (主) — 'Great Master of the Land,' the deity who built and ruled the terrestrial realm before ceding it (kuni-yuzuri). His alternate name Ōnamuchi (大穴牟遅) is older and obscure, perhaps opo 'great' + na (a name-element) + muchi/mochi (an honorific for high deities, as in Michi-nushi); the title Daikoku (大黒) is a later Buddhist-syncretic reading equating him with Mahākāla. Kuni 'land' and nushi 'lord' are basic Old Japanese.

linguistic.languageFamily: Japonic (Sino-Japanese compound) and native Old Japanese (Watatsumi)
linguistic.etymology: 龍神 Ryūjin, the Sino-Japanese reading of 龍 ryū 'dragon' (Middle Chinese *ljowng) + 神 jin 'god' — 'dragon god,' a designation overlaid on the older native sea-deity Watatsumi (綿津見 / 海神). Watatsumi parses as wata 'sea' (an old Japonic word for the sea, cf. wata-tsu-umi) + tsu (the archaic genitive particle) + mi 'spirit, body, august being' (cf. the -mi in many theonyms) — 'the spirit/lord of the sea.' Ō-watatsumi prefixes ō 'great.' The dragon (ryū) identity is a Sinitic/Buddhist overlay; the indigenous name is the wata-tsu-mi 'sea-spirit.'

sources.reference: Omodaka et al., Jidaibetsu Kokugo Daijiten: Jōdai-hen (1967), s.v. wata 'sea', -tu (genitive), mi

linguistic.etymology: 須佐之男命 Susanoo-no-Mikoto (full form Takehaya-Susanoo). The name is debated. The traditional Nihon Shoki gloss connects susa to the verb susabu/susamu 'to rage, be wild, act with violence,' giving 'the raging/impetuous male' (-no-o = no 'of' + o 'male, man,' 男) — apt for the storm-god. An alternative ties Susa to the place-name Susa (in Izumo), 'the man of Susa.' The honorifics in the full name are take 'brave, valiant' + haya 'swift, impetuous' (速). The kanji 須佐之男 are largely phonographic except 男 'male.'

claims.notes: Musubi is the hard word here and it has no English equivalent: it is the force by which things come into being and are tied to one another, and it is the reason the same syllable appears in the word for a knot and in the name of the deity of marriage-ties. Two of the first five kami are musubi deities, which places generation itself at the top of the Shinto cosmology — before any god who does anything. linguistic.etymology: 月読命 Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto, the moon-deity born from Izanagi's right eye. The name is transparently tsuku/tsuki 'moon' (月, Old Japanese tuku- in compounds, tukï) + yomi 'reading, counting, reckoning' (読み, from yomu 'to count, read, recite') — 'moon-reckoning,' i.e. the counting of months/the lunar calendar, personifying the moon as keeper of the count of nights. An older reading takes yomi as 'night-watch' or links it to the lunar measuring of time; the calendrical 'moon-counter' sense is standard. The characters 月読 directly write 'moon-read.'

sources.claim: Dezau (ḍezáw) is the supreme creator/sky god of the still-practised Kalash religion, also called Khodai; his name derives from PIE *dheigh- 'to fashion', and he has a female counterpart Dezalik.

sources.reference: Witzel, M. (2004). Kalash Religion (extract from The Rgvedic Religious System and its Central Asian and Hindukush Antecedents).
Cacopardo, A.M. & Cacopardo, A.S. (2001). Gates of Peristan.

faculties.name: fashions the world and the lesser gods
faculties.notes: Supreme creator; the root of his name (*dheigh, 'to mould/form') marks him as the fashioner. A distant high god, less ritually active than the Indra-figures and Mahandeo.

sources.reference: Witzel, M. (2004). Kalash Religion.

linguistic.etymology: Kalasha Dezau (ḍezáw), the creator god, identified with the Nuristani supreme creator Imrā. Witzel derives the theonym from Proto-Indo-European *dheiǵh- 'to form, to shape, to build', the same root that yields Vedic dih- and, more immediately, the Kati (Nuristani) verb dez 'to create' (Turner, Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages [CDIAL] no. 14621); the god is thus the 'Shaper/Maker'. The name is used interchangeably in Kalasha with the borrowed Persian/Pashto epithet Khodái 'God'.

sources.reference: Witzel, Michael. 'The Ṛgvedic Religious System and its Central Asian and Hindukush Antecedents.' In A. Griffiths & J.E.M. Houben (eds.), The Vedas: Texts, Language and Ritual (Proceedings of the Third International Vedic Workshop, Leiden 2002), Groningen: Egbert Forsten, 2004 (cited in the worklist as Witzel 2004, 'Kalash Religion').
R. L. Turner, A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages (London: Oxford University Press, 1962-66), entry 14621 (PIE *dheiǵh- 'to form'), as cited by Witzel for ḍezáw.

relations.subject: kalash_indr

sources.reference: Michael Witzel, 'The Ṛgvedic Religious System and its Central Asian and Hindukush Antecedents' (2004); Karl Jettmar, Die Religionen des Hindukusch (1975)

relations.notes: A cognate survival, not a borrowing: Kalasha Índr/Warín continues the Indo-Aryan storm-and-rain god (rainbow = 'Indra's bow'). The soma cult and deva-kingship are gone; he persists as weather-lord.

sources.claim: Indr/Warin is the Kalash storm-god, the mightiest and most dangerous deity, appearing in several Indra-forms - Warendr, Sajigor (Shura Verin) and Munjem Malik (Lord of Middle Earth, who slays his father) - preserving Rigvedic Indra motifs.

citations.reference: Witzel, M. (2004). Kalash Religion. Groningen: Forsten.
Jettmar, K. (1986). The Religions of the Hindukush, vol. 1. Aris & Phillips.

claims.notes: Kalasha índr/warín; the most conservatively Indo-Aryan of the Kalash gods. Munjem 'middle', malék < Arabic malik 'king'. The 'earth-and-underworld' domain covers his Munjem Malik (Middle Earth) aspect.

sources.reference: Witzel, M. (2004). Kalash Religion.
Witzel, M. (2004). Kalash Religion.
A. Witzel, 'The Religions of the Hindukush'; Kalash 'Indra's bow' (rainbow) tradition

faculties.name: wields the storm as the most dangerous of gods
faculties.notes: The Kalash Indra is splintered into forms - Warin (the mightiest, most dangerous), Sajigor/Shura Verin, and Munjem Malik (Lord of Middle Earth).

sources.reference: Witzel, M. (2004). Kalash Religion.

faculties.name: slays his father to win the middle earth
faculties.notes: As Munjem Malik he kills his father (a Vedic Indra motif) to become Lord of Middle Earth.

sources.reference: Witzel, M. (2004). Kalash Religion.

materialCulture.name: Indra's Bow (the rainbow)
materialCulture.notes: The bow of the Kalasha storm-god Warin/Indr: the rainbow is called 'Indra's bow' as in the Vedic tradition, the god's eagle is shot at, and the site of his shrine was fixed by a bow-shot, all marking the bow as his signature weapon.

sources.reference: Michael Witzel, 'The Rgvedic Religious System and its Central Asian and Hindukush Antecedents' (Kalash Religion section), in A. Griffiths & J.E.M. Houben (eds.), Groningen: Forsten, 2004, pp. 581-636

attributes.name: The rainbow as Indra's bow
attributes.notes: The rainbow is named 'Indra's bow' as in the Veda, and thunder is Indra at play; Warīn's shrine site was fixed by a bow-shot, echoing the Vedic Indra's bow.

sources.reference: A. Witzel, 'The Religions of the Hindukush'

linguistic.etymology: Kalasha Indr (also índr) is, per Witzel, the direct living reflex of Vedic Indra and the most conservatively Indo-Aryan figure in the Kalash pantheon, retaining Indra's rainbow, eagle, father-slaying and sun-releasing mythemes. A variant form Warén̄(dr-)/werín (also In Warín) is explained by Witzel as continuing *aparendra 'the unrivalled Indra'. His chthonic aspect Munjem Malik 'Lord of Middle Earth' shows munjem < Old Indo-Aryan *madhyama 'middle' compounded with the Arabic loan malék < malik 'king'.

sources.reference: Witzel, Michael. 'The Ṛgvedic Religious System and its Central Asian and Hindukush Antecedents.' In The Vedas: Texts, Language and Ritual, Groningen: Egbert Forsten, 2004 (worklist: Witzel 2004, 'Kalash Religion').
Jettmar, Karl. The Religions of the Hindukush, vol. 1: The Religion of the Kafirs. Warminster: Aris & Phillips, 1986 (on Indr/Indra continuity in the Hindu Kush).

linguistic.etymology: Kalasha Mahandeo (mahandéo), the god of crops who is also a war-god and the intermediary/negotiator with the supreme deity, corresponding to the Nuristani deity Mon/Māndi. Witzel reconstructs the name from *mahān deva, i.e. ultimately Sanskrit Mahādeva 'great god'; despite this Sanskritic etymology the figure is the indigenous Hindu Kush crop-and-war deity, not the Puranic Śiva. A.S. Cacopardo independently treats this figure and his sanctuary (the Kalasha 'Temple of Mahandeu', mythologically identified with the Nuristani 'Temple of Imrā').

names.value: Hetchhakuppa, Founder of the Agricultural Age
A Rai (Khambu) Mundhum name for the youngest child of Sumnima and Paruhang, remembered as the originator of cultivation and of the founding dances of the Kirat-Rai.

sources.claim: Hetchhakuppa is the youngest child of the Rai primordial pair Paruhang and Sumnima, remembered in Mundhum as the founder of the agricultural age and originator of the ancestral founding dance of the Kirat-Rai.

citations.reference: Martin Gaenszle, Ancestral Voices: Oral Ritual Texts and their Social Contexts among the Mewahang Rai of East Nepal (Münster: LIT Verlag, 2002)
Iman Singh Chemjong, History and Culture of the Kirat People, Parts I–II (Kathmandu: Kirat Yakthung Chumlung, 4th ed. 2003 [1967])

claims.notes: In the Rai (Khambu) branch of Kirati tradition Hetchhakuppa, also called Khakchhilip or Raichhakule, is the youngest child of the sky-father Paruhang and the earth-mother Sumnima and younger brother of the primeval sisters Tayama and Khiyama. He is honoured as the culture-hero who began the age of cultivation and who first performed the founding dance from which the Sakela dance-cycle is traced, making him a key ancestral progenitor of Kirat-Rai civilization.

claims.notes: Korean supreme heavenly ruler; lord of heaven in the Tangun foundation myth as preserved in the Samguk Yusa (1281 CE). Father of Hwanung the heavenly prince who descended to Mt. Taebaek (often identified with Mt. Baekdu on the modern Korea-China border); grandfather of Tangun, founder of Gojoseon. Hwanin granted his son Hwanung permission to descend to earth and bestowed three heavenly seals — a bell, a mirror, and a sword — as the regalia of divine kingship. (The mirror-sword-jewel triad is a wider East Asian sacral-kingship motif also present in the Japanese imperial regalia.) In modern Korean religion, Hwanin is identified with Hanullim ("Lord of Heaven") and Sangje, and is the central deity of Daejongism (a 20th-c. revival movement worshipping the Hwanin-Hwanung-Tangun trinity).

linguistic.etymology: 환인 / 桓因 Hwanin, the heavenly lord of the Tangun myth in the Samguk Yusa (1281). The monk Iryŏn glosses the name himself, equating Hwanin with 帝釋 Jeseok — i.e. Śakra/Indra (Sanskrit Śakra devānām indra), 因 standing for the 釋提桓因 Seokjehwanin transcription of Śakra-devānām-indra used in Buddhist texts. On this reading 桓因 Hwanin is a clipping of that Buddhist transcription of Indra's title. The native Korean equivalents Haneullim / Hanunim 'Lord of Heaven' (from 하늘 haneul 'sky, heaven' + the honorific -nim) reflect an indigenous sky-god identification onto which the Buddhist name was mapped.

Baekdu) with three heavenly seals (bell, mirror, sword) and 3,000 followers, establishing the sinsi ("divine city") at the sacred sandalwood tree (Sindansu). Established 360 affairs of human life — agriculture, lifespan, illness, punishment, good and evil — making him the foundational civilizing deity of Korean tradition. Transformed a bear into the woman Ungnyeo (after her 100-day cave-vigil with mugwort and garlic) and took human form to marry her; their son was Tangun, founder of Gojoseon. The hongik-ingan principle ("broadly benefiting humanity") associated with Hwanung is enshrined in modern South Korean educational law as a foundational national value. Worshipped as the second member of the Hwanin-Hwanung-Tangun trinity in modern Daejongism.

The graphs are read in Sino-Korean as 桓 hwan 'vigorous, martial, great; a marker shared with his father Hwanin' + 雄 ung 'male, hero, masculine, valiant' (the same 雄 as in 英雄 yeongung 'hero'). claims.notes: Korean foundation-figure; demigod son of Hwanung (the heavenly prince, son of Hwanin) by Ungnyeo (the bear transformed into a woman). Founded Gojoseon, the first Korean kingdom, traditionally dated 2333 BCE (the 50th year of the legendary Chinese Emperor Yao's reign per Samguk Yusa). Reigned 1,908 years per the literary tradition (Methuselah-syndrome inflation). After his reign, became a mountain spirit (sansin) at Mt. Asadal. The Tangun foundation myth survives in its earliest extant form in the Samguk Yusa (1281 CE), compiled by the Buddhist monk Iryeon during the Mongol-controlled Goryeo period; Iryeon explicitly cites the now-lost Gogi (Old Record) and a now-lost reference in the Wei chronicles. Pai 2000 (Constructing "Korean" Origins) reads the Samguk Yusa's Tangun-opening as a subtle resistance-message asserting Korean origins independent of Chinese authority during the Mongol occupation. Many Korean historians have argued for an etymological identity between Tangun and the Inner Asian Tengri (sky-god). 3 October is celebrated as Gaecheonjeol ("Opening of Heaven Day"), the South Korean national holiday commemorating Tangun's founding. Daejongism (founded 1909) is a modern Korean revival religion centered on the Hwanin-Hwanung-Tangun trinity. North Korea in 1993 announced the "discovery" of Tangun's remains and built a large mausoleum at Pyongyang (1994) — a politically-charged DPRK national-historical monument. The structural classification under the registry: ½ demigod (Hwanung as the divine pantheon-parent + Ungnyeo as the mortal partner — Ungnyeo is bear-transformed-into-fully-human at the time of Tangun's conception).

linguistic.etymology: 단군왕검 / 檀君王儉 Tangun Wanggeom, founder of Gojoseon. 檀君 Tangun: 檀 dan 'sandalwood / the birch-leaf pak tree (Betula); altar-tree' + 君 gun 'lord, prince.' Many scholars read 檀君 as a Sinographic transcription of an indigenous shamanic title — connecting tan- to a word for a sacred tree/altar or, on a widely cited proposal, to a Northeast-Asian/Altaic term for 'sky/Heaven' or 'shaman' (cf. Mongolic tengri 'sky,' and Korean dangol/tangol 'shaman'). 王儉 Wanggeom: 王 wang 'king' + 儉 geom (here a phonetic transcription, perhaps of an indigenous *kŏm 'ruler/divine,' cf. 곰 gom 'bear' and the divine-bear ancestress motif). The name thus encodes a priest-king title; the indigenous substrate of tan-/geom is debated.

claims.notes: Korean foundation-myth figure; originally a bear, transformed into a woman through 100-day cave-endurance on mugwort and garlic per Hwanung's instruction. The tiger that attempted the same vigil failed and gave up. Named Ungnyeo ("Bear-Woman") upon transformation. Prayed under the sacred Sindansu (sandalwood tree) for a child; Hwanung took human form to marry her; bore Tangun, founder of Gojoseon. Scholarly interpretation (per Pai, Constructing "Korean" Origins, 2000): the bear-tiger pairing represents two ancient clan-totems competing for the heavenly prince's favor, with the bear-clan emerging as the maternal lineage of the Korean people. Ungnyeo is bear-transformed-into-fully-human; at the time of Tangun's conception she is human, and so Tangun's demigod classification follows the standard rule (divine pantheon-parent + mortal partner). The bear is interpreted in Korean traditional cosmology as god-of-the-land and womb-of-products-of-farming-culture, complementing the sky-god paternal lineage in the Korean sacral-kingship hieros gamos pattern.

claims.notes: Batara Guru is the supreme sky deity of Malay folk cosmology, a Malay reflex of the Hindu god Shiva absorbed through the Srivijaya and Majapahit strata of Indianised belief and preserved under a later Islamic surface. He presides over kayangan, the upperworld, at the summit of a spirit hierarchy descending through mambang and jinn to the hantu of earth and water, and his name is spoken at the height of the bomoh's and pawang's invocations as lord of the heavens and giver of sacred knowledge.
