linguistic.etymology: Эрлэг хаан Erleg qaγan, lord and judge of the dead. The name is a loan from Old Turkic Erklig, originally an adjective 'mighty, powerful, having authority' (from Old Turkic erk 'power, authority, free will' + the possessive/adjectival suffix -lig) — 'the Powerful One,' a euphemistic title for the death-god. In the Old Turkic Buddhist/Manichaean texts Erklig Qan already names the ruler of the underworld (equated with Yama), and the term passed into Mongolic as Erlig. His Buddhist title Erlig Nomun Khan adds nom 'doctrine, dharma' (itself a loan, ultimately from Greek nomos via Sogdian) — 'Erlig, King of the Law,' i.e. Yama Dharmarāja.

linguistic.languageFamily: Tibeto-Mongol; the name a loan ultimately from Latin Caesar
linguistic.etymology: གེ་སར Ge-sar / Гэсэр Geser, hero-king of Ling. The name Gesar is generally derived from the title Caesar (Latin Caesar 'emperor') as it travelled across Asia: via the form by which the Eastern Roman/Byzantine and then the Iranian and Turkic worlds knew a great Western emperor — attested e.g. in connection with Phrom/Khrom (= Rome) and the 'Phrom Ge-sar,' the 'Caesar of Rome,' a title later attached to the epic hero. (A folk Tibetan reading links ge-sar to the word for the 'pistil/heart of a flower,' Sanskrit kesara, but the Caesar etymology is the dominant scholarly account.) Mongolian Geser Khan inherits the Tibetan form.

linguistic.languageFamily: Mongolic; loan ultimately from Iranian (Sogdian) Ahura Mazdā
linguistic.etymology: Хормуста тэнгэр Qormusta Tngri, head of the ninety-nine tngri (sky-gods). The name is a loan, through Sogdian/Uyghur Buddhist-Manichaean channels, of the Iranian high-god name Ahura Mazdā / Middle Persian Ohrmazd — Sogdian Xwrmzt(ʾ) — which in the Turco-Mongol Buddhist milieu became the name of the chief of the heaven-gods (there equated with Indra/Śakra as lord of the Tuṣita or Trāyastriṃśa heaven). Tngri/tenger means 'sky, heaven, sky-god.' So Qormusta Tngri is '(the) sky-god Ohrmazd,' an Iranian theonym naturalized as the Mongol king of the celestial deities.

linguistic.etymology: Nuristani Bagisht (Kamviri Bagišt; Prasun forms attested across dialects), god of flowing/flood waters and prosperity, in myth born in the current of the Prasun river, whereupon the turbulent waters became smooth and parted for the infant. Vedic Bhaga), fitting his role as a god of water-borne abundance; the precise reconstruction remains debated among Nuristani specialists.

linguistic.etymology: Nuristani Disani (Kamviri Disâni; Prasun Dízane/Dísni; with cognate forms Dísëňi, Dízëňi, Dísëi, Dísën̆i across Kata-vari/Waigali dialects; cognate with Kalasha Dezane/Dezalik), the great mother/fertility goddess. linguistic.etymology: கொற்றவை Koṟṟavai, the ancient Tamil goddess of war and victory of the arid pālai land. The name is built on the Old Tamil noun koṟṟam (கொற்றம்) 'victory, triumph, sovereignty, kingship' + the feminine suffix -avai/-ai — 'the (goddess of) Victory,' i.e. 'She of Triumph.' The root koṟṟ- 'victory/sovereignty' is well attested in Sangam Tamil (cf. koṟṟavan 'victorious king'). She is thus literally 'the Victorious Lady,' patroness of the battlefield, later assimilated to Durgā/Kālī. Mother of Murugan in Tamil tradition.

linguistic.etymology: மாரியம்மன் Māriyammaṉ, the folk mother-goddess of rain, fertility and epidemic disease. The name compounds māri (மாரி) 'rain; (the) rains' (Tamil/Dravidian māri 'rain, rainy season,' also by extension applied to smallpox/pestilence as her visitation) + ammaṉ / ammā (அம்மன்/அம்மா) 'mother, lady' (the Dravidian nursery word for 'mother,' used as the honorific for goddesses) — 'the Mother of Rain' / 'Rain-Mother.' She both sends rain and controls (or inflicts) epidemic fevers. Both elements — māri 'rain' and ammā 'mother' — are securely Dravidian.

linguistic.etymology: மாயோன் Māyōṉ, the 'dark god' of the pastoral mullai land in Sangam religion (later identified with Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa). The name derives from the Tamil colour-root mā / māy- 'dark, black, of dark hue' + the masculine singular suffix -ōṉ 'he who is' — 'the Dark One.' His synonym Māl (மால்) likewise means 'the dark/great one' (and 'bewilderment'), and Netiyōṉ 'the tall one' (neṭu- 'long, tall'). The dark complexion underlies the later equation with the blue-black Kṛṣṇa. The element mā- 'dark/black' is a basic Dravidian colour term.

linguistic.etymology: முருகன் Murukaṉ, the ancient Tamil god of the hill-country (kuṟiñci), war and youthful beauty, called the 'god of the Tamils.' The name derives from the Tamil noun muruku (முருகு) 'youth, beauty, fragrance, divinity, tender freshness' + the masculine suffix -aṉ — 'the Beautiful/Youthful One,' 'He of muruku.' The word muruku in Sangam usage denotes both 'beauty/youth' and the numinous/divine frenzy, so the name captures his nature as the ever-young, beautiful, ecstatic deity. His Sanskritic names (Skanda स्कन्द, Kārttikeya, Subrahmaṇya) are a later equation. The root muruku is securely Dravidian.

linguistic.etymology: พระแม่ธรณี Phra Mae Thorani, the Earth Goddess of the hair-wringing legend. Phra (พระ) is the Thai honorific for sacred/royal beings (itself ultimately from Sanskrit vara 'excellent' via Khmer braḥ); mae (แม่) is the native Tai word 'mother.' Thorani (ธรณี) is a Pali/Sanskrit loan, dharaṇī (धरणी) 'the earth, that which bears/supports' (from dhṛ- / dhar- 'to hold, bear'), so the core literally means 'the Bearer, the Earth.' Her Sanskrit name is Vasundharā (वसुन्धरा) 'wealth-bearing (earth).' Thus 'the Lady Mother Earth,' Tai honorific + native 'mother' + Indic 'earth.'

linguistic.etymology: དཔལ་ལྡན་ལྷ་མོ་ dpal ldan lha mo, the wrathful protectress of Tibet. The name is a Tibetan calque of Sanskrit श्रीदेवी Śrīdevī. Tibetan dpal 'glory, splendour, majesty' + ldan 'possessing, endowed with' = dpal-ldan 'glorious, the glorious one' — rendering Sanskrit śrī 'glory, splendour, the goddess Śrī.' Lha-mo 'goddess' (lha 'god, deity' + the feminine -mo) renders devī 'goddess.' So 'the Glorious Goddess.' Her epithet Magzor Gyalmo (dmag zor rgyal mo) means 'Queen who repels armies' (dmag 'army' + zor 'a hurled weapon/repelling power' + rgyal-mo 'queen'). The calque maps Tibetan dpal-ldan lha-mo onto Sanskrit Śrī-devī element for element.

linguistic.etymology: གཤིན་རྗེ་ gshin rje, the Tibetan form of Yama, lord of death. The name is a Tibetan calque/translation: gshin 'the dead, a dead person, deceased' + rje 'lord, master' — 'Lord of the Dead.' His title ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་པོ་ chos kyi rgyal po renders Sanskrit धर्मराज Dharmarāja 'King of the Dharma/Law': chos 'dharma, religious law' (the standard Tibetan translation of dharma) + kyi (genitive) + rgyal-po 'king' — 'King of the Religious Law.' Thus the Tibetan names map element-for-element onto Yama's Indic epithets (Lord of the dead / Dharmarāja). His wrathful form is Kālarūpa.

priesthoods.title: The kam (shaman) of the Altai and the sky-sacrifice ascent to Bay Ulgen
priesthoods.period: Documented 19th-early 20th c. (Altai Turks)
priesthoods.notes: Radloff and Anokhin recorded the Altai-Turkic kam's great horse-sacrifice, in which the shaman, over successive nights, ritually climbed the notched birch through the heavens to present the soul of the sacrificed horse to Bay Ulgen, the benevolent sky-god, and bring back his answer; the rite is the classic deity-directed shamanic liturgy of the Altai.

sources.reference: Wilhelm Radloff, Aus Sibirien (1884), description of the Altai sky-sacrifice
A. V. Anokhin, Materialy po shamanstvu u altaitsev (1924); Mircea Eliade, Shamanism (1964), ch. on the Altaic ascent

festivals.name: The Altai horse-sacrifice ascent to Bay Ülgen
festivals.notes: The Altaian kam (shaman) conducts the great horse-sacrifice in which, over successive nights, he ritually ascends through the heavens to present the soul of a light-coloured horse to Bay Ülgen, lord of the upper world; the classic description of the multi-night ascent is given by Radloff and analysed by Eliade.

sources.reference: Wilhelm Radloff, Aus Sibirien (1884), the Altaian horse-sacrifice to Bai Ülgän
Mircea Eliade, Shamanism: Archaic Techniques of Ecstasy (1951/1964), ch. on the Altaic ascent to Bai Ülgän

festivals.name: The white horse-sacrifice and shaman's ascent
festivals.notes: An Altai kam set up a yurt enclosing a young birch notched with steps (tapty); a white horse was sacrificed and the shaman, mounting its soul, climbed the heavens stage by stage to lay the offering before Bai Ülgen.

sources.reference: Wilhelm Radloff, Aus Sibirien; Mircea Eliade, Shamanism

discoveries.name: Sadashiva, Nilalohita, Rudra, Ardhanarishvara, Nataraja, Mallikarjuna, Bhairava/Kalabhairava/Kalaraja; Dakshinamurti, eleven Rudras and further incarnations
discoveries.decision: Reviewed forms linked or retained as same-record names. The Rigvedic portrayal and narrated Bhairava manifestation have explicit records. Further forms and their textual variants remain research, not automatically additional people.

discoveries.name: Oath, spouse and manifestation passage inventory
discoveries.decision: Ichiki-shima-hime/Sa-yori-bime, Tagi-tsu-hime, Ta-kiri-bime/Oki-tsu-shima; Suseri-bime, Yakami-hime, Ki-no-mata/Mi-wi, Nunakawa-hime all have explicit endpoints. Five jewel-born male oath children remain contextual discoveries: Ame-no-oshi-ho-mimi, Ame-no-hohi, Amatsu-hiko-ne, Iku-tsu-hiko-ne, Kumanu-kusubi; no guessed endpoint or imported family. Kartikeya carriers and six unnamed wives other than Arundhati are not biological parents. Mahakali portrayal retained on existing Kali; fevers/humours not inferred children. Nandi narrative locations Jatodaka, Trisrotas, Vrishadhvani, Svarnodaka, Jambunadi, Panchanada/Japesvara are places, not people.

discoveries.name: Nihongi I additional names
discoveries.decision: Iso-takeru/Isaoshi, Oho-ya-tsu-hime, Tsuma-tsu-hime, Sukuna-biko-na/Sukuna-hiko-na, Oho-mono-nushi, Mizo-kuhi-hime/Tama-kushi-hime and Hime-tatara I-suzu-hime have explicit records. Susa-no-yatsu-mimi has conflicting parental gender/context in adjacent accounts; retained as a textual discovery rather than merged with Ashinazuchi or Tenazuchi. Suga-no-yu-yama-nushi/Mitsu-na-saro-hiko and alternate long child names require independent identity review. Ama-no-Fuki-ne is a named distant descendant, not an invented intermediate parent. Kuye-biko and tani-guku are narrative informants, not family. Clan Kimi of Kamo/Oho-miwa are not converted to individual gods.

discoveries.name: Accessible collateral research
discoveries.decision: Oath daughters and Okuninushi spouse narratives now implemented from Kojiki XIII–XIV and XXI–XXV; Kartikeya’s carriers and Virabhadra’s manifestation are now cited. Nihongi direct parentage and generation variants, Ukanomitama and Sukunabikona conflicting parents, tree-planting children, Miwa cult portrayal and Isuzuhime accounts are now implemented. Kartikeya regional spouses, further Shiva forms, and legacy powers/objects/rituals throughout the frontier still require passage review. These are unfinished work, not access blockers.
